section.title: Introduction
section.p: Adjectives describe what something or someone is like, for example how it or they look. Most adjectives can be used both attributively, as in Dïhte lea 'besteles' nejpie. (It is a sharp knife.) and 'besteles' nejpie. (a sharp knife), and predicatively, as in ?? '???'. (The knife is sharp.)
An adjective takes the attributive form when it precedes the noun and the predicative form when it follows the noun and the verb “be”. These forms can differ.

section.title: Degrees of comparison
section.p: Adjectives can also be inflected for degree, for example stoere - stuerebe - stööremes (big – bigger – biggest). The forms may use a different stem or form a new one. See the chapter on adjective derivation.

section.title: Case and number
section.p: Attributive adjectives do not agree with the noun, for example ?? But if … An adjective can be used as a noun and is then inflected in all cases. South Sámi has eight cases. The inflection pattern is the same as for nouns, for example ??
Predicative adjectives agree with the noun in number, for example ??

section.title: Other features
section.p: Adjectives can change form when they are inflected. They take different inflectional endings, and the stem may also change. Stem changes such as vowel alternation, consonant gradation and palatalization are covered in the chapter on morphophonology.

Inflectional endings also exhibit allomorphy, meaning that they have variant forms. The adjective’s inflection class determines the inflectional stem and endings, while the subgroup (A, B or C) determines how the stem vowel changes. Here you can read more about noun inflection and inflection classes.
